newsitem.title: UK: Britain's socialists, left out and left behind.
newsitem.headline: Britain's socialists, left out and left behind.

text.p: Britain's "reds" have a problem. The Labour party has turned purple.

Formed at the start of the century to protect the rights of the workers, Britain's main opposition party has ditched most of its left-wing policies under the leadership of Tony Blair in a bid to regain power after nearly two decades in the political wilderness.

"New Labour" has embraced privatisation, distanced itself from the trade unions which once provided its foundations and promised to abandon its traditional tax-and-spend economic policies in favour of fiscal discipline.
Britain's hard-line socialists are appalled.

"Labour never mentions the poor, the needy, the workers. They don't exist for Blair. He speaks to businessmen and businesswomen and the poor have been forsaken," said Tony Cliff, founder of the Socialist Workers' Party (SWP).

Many socialists say they have been left out of British politics, abandoned by Labour and with no major party to give them a voice. They say the workers who founded Labour have been brushed aside in Blair's eagerness to win middle-class votes.
"We are the grass roots of the Labour Party. Our forefathers founded it," said Mickey Tighe, one of 329 sacked Liverpool dockers fighting to win back their jobs.
Labour has shown little support for their campaign and plans to leave in place many anti-union policies of the ruling Conservatives if, as expected, it wins the May 1 general election.
The dockers, and many other socialists, feel betrayed.
Labour has even decided to adopt the colour purple for many of its posters, pamphlets and backdrops as the election approaches, cutting down on traditionally socialist red.
WAITING FOR THE REVOLUTION
Communism may have collapsed in Eastern Europe but the hard left still believes Britain's revolution is on the way.

"We must fan the flames of rage and anger that exist in society into a furnace to burn the capitalist society down," campaigning journalist Paul Foot told a Socialist Workers' Party rally in London's impoverished East End this month to cheers from the 200 "comrades" in the hall.
Labour's rightward lurch has spawned several parties hoping to win disgruntled socialists' votes and hasten the revolution.
The group fielding the most candidates is the Socialist Labour Party founded by former union boss Arthur Scargill.

Contesting more than 60 seats, the party demands an 80 percent tax-band for the rich, a wholesale nationalisation of industry and complete withdrawal from the European Union. It believes a four-day week would help to eliminate unemployment.
The party won more than five percent of the vote in a by-election last year and is the left's best hope of poll success although its chances of winning any seats are minimal.
The Militant Tendency, a Trotskyite group founded in the 1950s which attempted to infiltrate the Labour Party, is fielding 27 candidates under the banner of the Socialist Party.
Labour's attempts to purge itself of Militant members in the 1980s convulsed the party and helped keep it out of power.

Britain still boasts a Communist Party, which is fielding three candidates. "We are still a communist party and we still want to see a communist Britain, although it might not be in my lifetime," said general election organiser Sandra Lusk.
"VOTE LABOUR AND TRY NOT TO PUKE"

Many hard-line socialists, however, believe there is little point in standing at the election. Tony Cliff of the Socialist Workers' Party said his party was not fighting on May 1 because small parties in British politics had as little hope of success as small clubs in British football.
"If Manchester United is playing Liverpool, there is no point jumping up and cheering for Fulham," he said. "Fulham is not playing. We're not even in the league."
Cliff believes Blair will win the election but face immense popular anger afterwards as workers realise his policies are little different from the right-wing Conservative Party.
"Blair will win but there will be such anger with Labour that there will be bloody battles," he said.

He advises voters to help secure a Labour victory, then try to drag the Labour Party back towards the left of politics. But he concedes that Blair's abandonment of so many socialist policies makes this advice harder to stomach.
"We used to say people should vote Labour but with no illusions," Cliff said. "Now I would have to say -- vote Labour and try not to puke (vomit)."

Cliff's advice is shared by the Communist Party, which advises voters to choose Labour when they have no communist candidate. "We want to see Labour re-elected and then shift them back to the left. That's the best way forward," Lusk said.
The hard left hopes that if Labour wins power, left-leaning politicians in the party will seize the chance to make their voices heard and reclaim Labour for hard-line socialism.

Some Labour members of parliament are known to be disgruntled about Blair's policy changes. A writer with the pseudonym "Cassandra", claimed to be a senior Labour politician, wrote in the left-wing Tribune newspaper last November that the move to the right would be resisted.

"While it has so far been only the hard left and Trotskyite grouplets who have been ranting on about these issues, once pre-election unity is no longer required all these changes have the potential to re-awaken..civil war," Cassandra wrote.
"Tony Blair's position as leader of the Labour Party is weaker than that of any leader in memory," Cassandra warned. "He could become the shortest-serving prime minister this century."
Britain's die-hard socialists have their fingers crossed.
